Encoding physical symmetries into these models can improve performance on difficult tasks, and recent work has motivated the principle of parameter symmetry breaking and restoration as a unifying mechanism underlying their hierarchical learning dynamics. We evaluate the role of parameter symmetry and network expressivity in the generalisation behaviour of neural networks when learning a real-space renormalisation group (RG) transformation, using the central limit theorem (CLT) as a test case map. We consider simple multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and graph neural networks (GNNs), and vary weight symmetries and activation functions across architectures. Our results reveal a competition between symmetry constraints and expressivity, with overly complex or overconstrained models generalising poorly. We analytically demonstrate this poor generalisation behaviour for certain constrained MLP architectures by recasting the CLT as a cumulant recursion relation and making use of an established framework to propagate cumulants through MLPs. We also empirically validate an extension of this framework from MLPs to GNNs, elucidating the internal information processing performed by these more complex models. These findings offer new insight into the learning dynamics of symmetric networks and their limitations in modelling structured physical transformations.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: XAI-Driven Deep Learning for Protein Sequence Functional Group Classification
papers.research_question: How do different deep learning architectures perform on protein functional group classification, and how can explainable AI techniques reveal biologically meaningful sequence motifs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a comparative deep learning framework for protein functional group classification, demonstrating that CNNs achieve the highest accuracy, and uses explainable AI techniques (Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients) to identify biologically relevant sequence motifs.
papers.conclusion: Deep learning architectures, particularly CNNs, can achieve high predictive accuracy for protein functional group classification, and explainable AI techniques successfully uncover biologically meaningful sequence motifs that align with known catalytic mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN model achieved the highest validation accuracy (91.8%) for protein functional group classification.
Explainable AI techniques revealed motifs enriched in histidine, aspartate, glutamate, and lysine, residues commonly associated with catalytic and metal-binding sites in enzymes.
Different architectures focus on motifs differently: CNNs emphasize localized motifs, BiLSTMs distribute relevance across broader regions, and attention-based models concentrate on a single discriminative subsequence.
The recurrence of specific motifs (e.g., HIDRL, HQLLH, DEEVK) across multiple architectures suggests the models learn conserved biochemical features rather than arbitrary patterns.
The integration of XAI bridges computational performance with biological interpretability, showing that the networks capture molecular logic governing enzyme function.
future_direction: Extending the framework to multi-functional enzyme prediction.
Validating identified motifs against structural and biochemical databases to strengthen the connection between model explanations and experimentally verified protein function.
papers.abstract: Proteins perform essential biological functions, and accurate classification of their sequences is critical for understanding structure-function relationships, enzyme mechanisms, and molecular interactions. This study presents a deep learning-based framework for functional group classification of protein sequences derived from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Four architectures were implemented: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM), CNN-BiLSTM hybrid, and CNN with Attention. Each model was trained using k-mer integer encoding to capture both local and long-range dependencies. Among these, the CNN achieved the highest validation accuracy of 91.8%, demonstrating the effectiveness of localized motif detection. Explainable AI techniques, including Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients, were applied to interpret model predictions and identify biologically meaningful sequence motifs. The discovered motifs, enriched in histidine, aspartate, glutamate, and lysine, represent amino acid residues commonly found in catalytic and metal-binding regions of transferase enzymes. These findings highlight that deep learning models can uncover functionally relevant biochemical signatures, bridging the gap between predictive accuracy and biological interpretability in protein sequence analysis.

papers.title: Engineering Monosemanticity in Toy Models
papers.research_question: How can we engineer monosemanticity in toy models? Specifically, can models be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by steering training to different minima, and how do bias and number of neurons affect monosemanticity?
papers.core_contribution: Models can be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by steering training to minima with moderate negative biases, and increasing the number of neurons per layer increases monosemanticity at the cost of compute.
papers.conclusion: Engineering monosemanticity in toy models is possible via negative biases and wider layers, pointing to future work on robust engineering and understanding polysemantic models.
papers.key_findings:
Models can be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by changing which local minimum training finds.
More monosemantic minima have moderate negative biases, enabling engineering of highly monosemantic models via negative bias initialization and weight decay.
Providing more neurons per layer makes models more monosemantic, albeit at increased computational cost.
In engineered monosemantic models, monosemantic neurons implement a simple algorithm balancing feature recovery against interference, and polysemantic neurons implement a low-rank linear map adjusting confidence.
The conclusions hold for various activation functions and feature frequency distributions.
papers.limitation:
The engineering approach is fragile because it depends on setting a bias weight decay rate that must be slow relative to the rate at which the model learns the task.
Naive introduction of sparsity in model weights results in significant reductions in task performance.
future_direction: Make the bias engineering more robust by tailoring bias decay per neuron or tying it to weight changes, or using regularizers.
Understand the algorithm implemented by highly polysemantic models.
Find ways to reduce compute cost of wider layers without excessive performance degradation.
papers.abstract: In some neural networks, individual neurons correspond to natural ``features'' in the input. Such \emph{monosemantic} neurons are of great help in interpretability studies, as they can be cleanly understood. In this work we report preliminary attempts to engineer monosemanticity in toy models. We find that models can be made more monosemantic without increasing the loss by just changing which local minimum the training process finds. More monosemantic loss minima have moderate negative biases, and we are able to use this fact to engineer highly monosemantic models. We are able to mechanistically interpret these models, including the residual polysemantic neurons, and uncover a simple yet surprising algorithm. Finally, we find that providing models with more neurons per layer makes the models more monosemantic, albeit at increased computational cost. These findings point to a number of new questions and avenues for engineering monosemanticity, which we intend to study these in future work.

papers.title: Mutagenesis screen to map the functions of parameters of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how to systematically map the connections between model parameters and their functionalities in large language models using a mutagenesis screening approach.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces mutagenesis screening as a method to map parameter functions in LLMs, revealing intricate structures, sensitive points, and creative 'writer' mutations in models like Llama2-7b and Zephyr.
papers.conclusion: The study successfully applies mutagenesis screening to LLMs, revealing features at multiple levels and opening new avenues for understanding and enhancing AI systems, with potential for broader application to other model types.
papers.key_findings:
Matrices in LLMs show bias towards maximum or minimum mutations, indicating intrinsic properties rather than input-specific responses.
Non-silent mutations (NSMs) cluster along specific rows and columns, revealing structural patterns and conserved sensitive points across layers.
Correlative Complementary Patterns (COPA) are observed where maximum and minimum mutations complement each other in matrices, with unique asymmetry in Gate matrices.
"Writer" mutations in Zephyr produce poetic or dialogic outputs, showing creative capabilities linked to specific parameter regions and row coordinates.
Sensitive points in matrices, such as column 39 in Llama2-7b and column 32 in Zephyr, significantly affect model performance when mutated, highlighting critical functional regions.
papers.limitation: The use of basic cosine similarity metrics provides minimal information from outputs, indicating a need for more sophisticated analytical methods to fully leverage mutagenesis screening data.
future_direction: Develop more sophisticated analytical methods for mutagenesis screening data.
Identify more mutations that produce novel outputs and delve deeper into the functions of specific elements in LLMs.
Apply mutagenesis screening to other large-scale models such as image and video generative models and multi-modal LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced artificial intelligence, excelling in numerous tasks. Although the functionality of a model is inherently tied to its parameters, a systematic method for exploring the connections between the parameters and the functionality are lacking. Models sharing similar structure and parameter counts exhibit significant performance disparities across various tasks, prompting investigations into the varying patterns that govern their performance. We adopted a mutagenesis screen approach inspired by the methods used in biological studies, to investigate Llama2-7b and Zephyr. This technique involved mutating elements within the models' matrices to their maximum or minimum values to examine the relationship between model parameters and their functionalities. Our research uncovered multiple levels of fine structures within both models. Many matrices showed a mixture of maximum and minimum mutations following mutagenesis, but others were predominantly sensitive to one type. Notably, mutations that produced phenotypes, especially those with severe outcomes, tended to cluster along axes. Additionally, the location of maximum and minimum mutations often displayed a complementary pattern on matrix in both models, with the Gate matrix showing a unique two-dimensional asymmetry after rearrangement. In Zephyr, certain mutations consistently resulted in poetic or conversational rather than descriptive outputs. These "writer" mutations grouped according to the high-frequency initial word of the output, with a marked tendency to share the row coordinate even when they are in different matrices. Our findings affirm that the mutagenesis screen is an effective tool for deciphering the complexities of large language models and identifying unexpected ways to expand their potential, providing deeper insights into the foundational aspects of AI systems.

papers.title: Rethinking LLM-as-a-Judge: Representation-as-a-Judge with Small Language Models via Semantic Capacity Asymmetry
papers.research_question: Can small language models serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations, even when their generation is poor?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis and introduces INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that extracts evaluation signals from small model representations, enabling efficient and accurate reference-free evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Small LMs retain strong evaluative signals in their internal representations, and the Representation-as-a-Judge paradigm via INSPECTOR offers a scalable and interpretable solution for evaluation and data curation.
papers.key_findings:
Small LMs encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states despite weak generation.
Probing internal representations with INSPECTOR outperforms prompt-based evaluation with small LMs and closely approximates large LLM judges.
The Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis is supported: evaluation requires less semantic capacity than generation.
Probing classifiers can serve as reliable data filters for supervised fine-tuning, leading to performance gains.
Larger LLMs do not necessarily provide stronger evaluation signals than smaller ones.
papers.limitation:
Multiclass prediction performance of probing classifiers is modest (50-60%) compared to binary classification.
Out-of-distribution generalization for multiclass probing is limited, with F1 scores dropping significantly.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as reference-free evaluators via prompting, but this "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm is costly, opaque, and sensitive to prompt design. In this work, we investigate whether smaller models can serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations instead of surface generation. We uncover a consistent empirical pattern: small LMs, despite with weak generative ability, encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states. This motivates us to propose the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis: evaluation requires significantly less semantic capacity than generation and can be grounded in intermediate representations, suggesting that evaluation does not necessarily need to rely on large-scale generative models but can instead leverage latent features from smaller ones. Our findings motivate a paradigm shift from LLM-as-a-Judge to Representation-as-a-Judge, a decoding-free evaluation strategy that probes internal model structure rather than relying on prompted output. We instantiate this paradigm through INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that predicts aspect-level evaluation scores from small model representations. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, GPQA) show that INSPECTOR substantially outperforms prompting-based small LMs and closely approximates full LLM judges, while offering a more efficient, reliable, and interpretable alternative for scalable evaluation.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Inducing Transformer's Compositional Generalization Ability via Auxiliary Sequence Prediction Tasks
papers.research_question: How can auxiliary sequence prediction tasks induce compositional generalization ability in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes auxiliary sequence prediction tasks to induce compositional generalization in Transformers, achieving perfect accuracy on challenging SCAN splits.
papers.conclusion: Auxiliary sequence prediction tasks can effectively induce compositional generalization in Transformers, with potential for few-shot learning and application to other datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Auxiliary sequence prediction enables Transformers to achieve 100% accuracy on SCAN MCD splits.
The method is sample-efficient, achieving 97.8% accuracy with only 5% training data.
Both auxiliary sequences are necessary for optimal performance.
Using less contextualized decoder vectors as queries improves compositional generalization.
The approach generalizes to the grounded-SCAN task.
papers.limitation:
SCAN is a synthetic dataset, so findings may not transfer to large-scale natural datasets.
Applying the method to natural language requires designing heuristics to approximate grammar.
future_direction: Using human-annotated auxiliary sequences for natural datasets.
papers.abstract: Systematic compositionality is an essential mechanism in human language, allowing the recombination of known parts to create novel expressions. However, existing neural models have been shown to lack this basic ability in learning symbolic structures. Motivated by the failure of a Transformer model on the SCAN compositionality challenge (Lake and Baroni, 2018), which requires parsing a command into actions, we propose two auxiliary sequence prediction tasks that track the progress of function and argument semantics, as additional training supervision. These automatically-generated sequences are more representative of the underlying compositional symbolic structures of the input data. During inference, the model jointly predicts the next action and the next tokens in the auxiliary sequences at each step. Experiments on the SCAN dataset show that our method encourages the Transformer to understand compositional structures of the command, improving its accuracy on multiple challenging splits from <= 10% to 100%. With only 418 (5%) training instances, our approach still achieves 97.8% accuracy on the MCD1 split. Therefore, we argue that compositionality can be induced in Transformers given minimal but proper guidance. We also show that a better result is achieved using less contextualized vectors as the attention's query, providing insights into architecture choices in achieving systematic compositionality. Finally, we show positive generalization results on the groundedSCAN task (Ruis et al., 2020). Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/jiangycTarheel/compositional-auxseq

papers.title: DGTN: Graph-Enhanced Transformer with Diffusive Attention Gating Mechanism for Enzyme DDG Prediction
papers.research_question: How can we accurately predict the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (∆∆G) by integrating sequence and structural information through a co-learning framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DGTN, a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network and transformer representations through a bidirectional diffusion mechanism for protein stability prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: DGTN effectively integrates 3D geometric and evolutionary sequence context through bidirectional diffusion, establishing a principled and interpretable paradigm for accurate protein stability prediction and design.
papers.key_findings:
DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance on ProTherm with Pearson correlation ρ=0.87 and RMSE=1.21 kcal/mol, outperforming existing baselines.
Ablation studies show the bidirectional diffusion mechanism contributes a 6-point gain in Pearson correlation over simple cross-modal fusion.
The model generalizes well to unseen datasets (SKEMPI, Ssym, FireProtDB), demonstrating robust learning of stability principles.
Theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to an optimal structure-aware attention matrix with a convergence rate of O(1/√T).
Attention visualization confirms the model successfully identifies spatially proximate but sequentially distant residue interactions.
papers.limitation:
Operates on a single static conformation of the wild-type protein, unable to capture dynamic or entropic contributions to stability.
Evaluates mutations in isolation and does not explicitly model epistatic (non-additive) interactions between multiple substitutions.
Training data (ProTherm) exhibits class imbalance, with certain protein families overrepresented, potentially limiting generalization.
future_direction: Incorporate ensembles of structures (from molecular dynamics or predicted distributions) to model flexibility and allostery.
Extend the architecture to jointly represent combinatorial mutations via graph-based mutation encoding or interaction-aware attention.
Improve robustness to dataset imbalance via domain-adversarial training, balanced sampling, or cross-family transfer learning.
papers.abstract: Predicting the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (DDG) is fundamental to protein engineering and drug design. While recent deep learning approaches have shown promise, they often process sequence and structure information independently, failing to capture the intricate coupling between local structural geometry and global sequential patterns. We present DGTN (Diffused Graph-Transformer Network), a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network (GNN) weights for structural priors and transformer attention through a diffusion mechanism. Our key innovation is a bidirectional diffusion process where: (1) GNN-derived structural embeddings guide transformer attention via learnable diffusion kernels, and (2) transformer representations refine GNN message passing through attention-modulated graph updates. We provide rigorous mathematical analysis showing this co-learning scheme achieves provably better approximation bounds than independent processing. On ProTherm and SKEMPI benchmarks, DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance (Pearson Rho = 0.87, RMSE = 1.21 kcal/mol), with 6.2% improvement over best baselines. Ablation studies confirm the diffusion mechanism contributes 4.8 points to correlation. Our theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to optimal structure-sequence coupling, with convergence rate O(1/sqrt(T) ) where T is diffusion steps. This work establishes a principled framework for integrating heterogeneous protein representations through learnable diffusion.

papers.title: Unveiling Latent Knowledge in Chemistry Language Models through Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do chemistry language models internally represent chemical knowledge, and can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features within these models?
papers.core_contribution: This work presents the first application of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to chemistry language models, revealing that these models encode a rich hierarchy of interpretable chemical features spanning structural motifs, physicochemical properties, and functional concepts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders can decompose the latent representations of a chemistry language model into an interpretable feature basis, revealing a rich landscape of chemically meaningful concepts and enabling causal manipulation of molecular structures.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features outperform individual neurons in detecting chemical substructures, especially rare ones, indicating a more disentangled representation.
SAE features provide a compact and decorrelated basis for aligning internal representations with external physicochemical descriptors.
Individual SAE features can capture higher-level functional concepts, such as grouping molecules by shared pharmacological activity (e.g., opioid receptor binding).
Feature steering via ablation demonstrates a causal link between specific features and the generation of corresponding chemical substructures or properties.
The SAE decomposition is information-preserving for downstream tasks (e.g., toxicity prediction) while isolating relevant signals into a more compact set of features than the original neuron basis.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of features remains a presently unscaled process.
The analysis is confined to a single model architecture (SMI-TED).
The features discovered are contingent on the training data's chemical space, and their generalisation to out-of-distribution molecules remains an open question.
While features are compared to the raw neuron basis, more robust baselines are needed to fully validate the decomposition's effectiveness.
future_direction: Developing methods for the automated interpretation of chemical features.
Exploring applications in AI safety, such as identifying and ablating features correlated with undesirable properties (e.g., toxicity).
Investigating how features behave across different model architectures and scales, including exploring concepts like feature splitting.
papers.abstract: Since the advent of machine learning, interpretability has remained a persistent challenge, becoming increasingly urgent as generative models support high-stakes applications in drug and material discovery. Recent advances in large language model (LLM) architectures have yielded chemistry language models (CLMs) with impressive capabilities in molecular property prediction and molecular generation. However, how these models internally represent chemical knowledge remains poorly understood. In this work, we extend sparse autoencoder techniques to uncover and examine interpretable features within CLMs. Applying our methodology to the Foundation Models for Materials (FM4M) SMI-TED chemistry foundation model, we extract semantically meaningful latent features and analyse their activation patterns across diverse molecular datasets. Our findings reveal that these models encode a rich landscape of chemical concepts. We identify correlations between specific latent features and distinct domains of chemical knowledge, including structural motifs, physicochemical properties, and pharmacological drug classes. Our approach provides a generalisable framework for uncovering latent knowledge in chemistry-focused AI systems. This work has implications for both foundational understanding and practical deployment; with the potential to accelerate computational chemistry research.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
Alleviating the dictionary training problem of dead neurons to achieve deeper understanding.
Extending the method to language models, which have sparser features and a more complex world compared to the Othello task.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: Explaining reaction coordinates of alanine dipeptide isomerization obtained from deep neural networks using Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)
papers.research_question: How can Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods explain which collective variables contribute to the reaction coordinates predicted by deep neural networks for alanine dipeptide isomerization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that XAI methods (LIME and SHAP) can provide local explanations for the contribution of collective variables to reaction coordinates predicted by a deep neural network for alanine dipeptide isomerization, revealing the importance of specific dihedral angles.
papers.conclusion: The proposed AI-aided method combined with XAI provides a practical tool for locally explaining appropriate reaction coordinates from DNN training, especially near the transition state, and is applicable to complex molecular systems.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks can be trained to predict appropriate reaction coordinates for alanine dipeptide isomerization.
Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation (LIME) and Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provide local explanations of feature contributions to the predicted reaction coordinates.
Near the transition state, the dihedral angle θ becomes more important than near the stable states, indicating its role in crossing the barrier.
The feature contributions from LIME and SHAP are consistent, justifying LIME's linear model assumption.
The method can identify dominant collective variables consistent with previous committor test analyses.
papers.limitation: Understanding the detailed mechanism for complex molecular systems becomes complicated because of the large numbers of collective variables.
future_direction: Application to solute-solvent systems such as alanine dipeptide in explicit water.
Application to various other solute-solvent systems.
papers.abstract: A method for obtaining appropriate reaction coordinates is required to identify transition states distinguishing the product and reactant in complex molecular systems. Recently, abundant research has been devoted to obtaining reaction coordinates using artificial neural networks from deep learning literature, where many collective variables are typically utilized in the input layer. However, it is difficult to explain the details of which collective variables contribute to the predicted reaction coordinates owing to the complexity of the nonlinear functions in deep neural networks. To overcome this limitation, we used Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods of the Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation (LIME) and the game theory-based framework known as Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). We demonstrated that XAI enables us to obtain the degree of contribution of each collective variable to reaction coordinates that is determined by nonlinear regressions with deep learning for the committor of the alanine dipeptide isomerization in vacuum. In particular, both LIME and SHAP provide important features to the predicted reaction coordinates, which are characterized by appropriate dihedral angles consistent with those previously reported from the committor test analysis. The present study offers an AI-aided framework to explain the appropriate reaction coordinates, which acquires considerable significance when the number of degrees of freedom increases.

papers.title: When the Coffee Feature Activates on Coffins: An Analysis of Feature Extraction and Steering for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does the approach of semantic feature extraction via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising route for AI safety, and how generalizable are the claims about interpretable features and feature steering made by Anthropic?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that while sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based feature extraction and steering can produce compelling demonstrations, the methods exhibit substantial fragility and context-dependence, falling short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE-based interpretability methods are not reliable enough for safety-critical applications, suggesting a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output.
papers.key_findings:
Feature steering is fragile, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context.
There exist non-standard activation behaviors (e.g., high activation density, disproportionate activation on the beginning-of-text token) that are not captured by automated feature interpretations.
It is difficult to distinguish thematically similar features from one another, even within the same layer.
Automated interpretations of features (labels) often do not align with the features' activation patterns across text samples or their effects when used for model steering.
SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases but current methods often lack systematic reliability.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to one publicly available model (Llama 3.1-8B) and a specific set of pre-trained SAEs (Llama Scope).
The study does not have internal access to Anthropic's proprietary models (e.g., Claude 3.0 Sonnet) and relies on the assumption of a weak form of universality.
future_direction: Future work should focus on reliable prediction and control of model output, rather than just interpretability of internal representations.
More research is needed to understand the conditions under which interpretable features emerge and to verify that they function computationally in ways analogous to human concepts.
papers.abstract: Recent work by Anthropic on Mechanistic interpretability claims to understand and control Large Language Models by extracting human-interpretable features from their neural activation patterns using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). If successful, this approach offers one of the most promising routes for human oversight in AI safety. We conduct an initial stress-test of these claims by replicating their main results with open-source SAEs for Llama 3.1. While we successfully reproduce basic feature extraction and steering capabilities, our investigation suggests that major caution is warranted regarding the generalizability of these claims. We find that feature steering exhibits substantial fragility, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context. We observe non-standard activation behavior and demonstrate the difficulty to distinguish thematically similar features from one another. While SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases, current methods often fall short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications. This suggests a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output. Our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of what mechanistic interpretability has achieved and highlights fundamental challenges for AI safety that remain unresolved.

papers.title: Efficient Representations are Controllable Representations
papers.research_question: What is the most brute-force way to install interpretable, controllable features into a model’s activations? Can a model's efficiency pressure be exploited to induce interpretable, controllable representations?
papers.core_contribution: By finetuning an LLM with a simple auxiliary loss to write binary feature classifications into a small set of residual stream dimensions, the model reorganizes to depend on these flags, making them genuine internal features that can be used to steer generation at inference time. This works due to the model's efficiency pressure under capacity constraints.
papers.conclusion: The residual stream is writable, and a model's own efficiency pressure can be exploited to induce interpretable and controllable representations. This inverts the usual controllability problem by providing signals that the model will naturally consolidate around.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns to write correct feature flags to the designated 'fenced' dimensions after training.
The model learns to depend on these flags during generation, as shown by overwriting experiments that causally steer generation.
The model erodes its own alternative representations of the fenced features, consolidating feature information into the fenced dimensions.
The efficiency pressure (representational cost) leads the model to consolidate around the reliably supplied feature signals.
The method incurs a negligible perplexity cost when fencing a small number of dimensions, but the cost grows as more dimensions are fenced.
papers.limitation:
Early layers (k < 5) struggle to produce clean flags, consistent with the view that early layers have not yet derived the relevant features.
At the current level of training, the model has begun to erode previous representations but some residual information persists in the remaining dimensions.
papers.abstract: What is the most brute-force way to install interpretable, controllable features into a model's activations? Controlling how LLMs internally represent concepts typically requires sophisticated methods to first identify, then intervene on the model's existing feature geometry. We bypass all of this. We finetune an LLM with a simple auxiliary loss, training 16 of its 3072 residual stream dimensions to be inert interpretability flags that simply indicate what concepts are required for generation. The model reorganizes around them anyway, learning to rely on these flags during actual generation tasks. As a result, these inert flags become genuine internal features: interpretable control switches that allow us to steer generation at inference time. Why does this work? When a feature is reliably supplied at a fixed location, gradient descent gradually eliminates redundant encodings elsewhere, and the model erodes its own alternative representations. A model's efficiency pressure is a lever - exploitable to induce interpretable, controllable representations.

papers.title: Steering Large Language Models using Conceptors: Improving Addition-Based Activation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can conceptors be used to improve the precision and effectiveness of activation engineering for steering large language models compared to traditional additive steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces conceptors as a novel steering mechanism for large language models, demonstrating that they provide more precise control and outperform traditional additive steering methods across multiple tasks.
papers.conclusion: Conceptor-based steering outperforms additive methods and offers a more precise and effective way to control LLM outputs, suggesting a shift towards region-based representations in activation engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Conceptor-based steering achieves higher accuracy than additive steering on all function tasks for both GPT-J and GPT-NeoX models.
Mean-centering enhances the performance of both steering methods, but conceptors still outperform even without mean-centering.
Conceptors can be combined using Boolean operations (AND) to steer composite functions, outperforming additive combination of steering vectors.
Steering is most effective in specific layers (9-16 for GPT-J, 10-30 for GPT-NeoX).
The aperture parameter α for conceptors is robust, with α=0.1 performing well across experiments.
papers.limitation:
Conceptors rely on more data points to build accurate representations.
Conceptors are more computationally expensive compared to simple addition-based methods.
Conceptors introduce a new hyperparameter, the aperture α, that may require tuning for optimal performance.
future_direction: Assess the impact of conceptor steering on the model's overall capabilities.
Evaluate performance on more complex behaviors or tasks.
Investigate scalability to larger models.
papers.abstract: Large language models have transformed AI, yet reliably controlling their outputs remains a challenge. This paper explores activation engineering, where outputs of pre-trained LLMs are controlled by manipulating their activations at inference time. Unlike traditional methods using a single steering vector, we introduce conceptors - mathematical constructs that represent sets of activation vectors as ellipsoidal regions. Conceptors act as soft projection matrices and offer more precise control over complex activation patterns. Our experiments demonstrate that conceptors outperform traditional methods across multiple steering tasks. We further use Boolean operations on conceptors for combined steering goals that empirically outperform additively combining steering vectors on a set of tasks. These results highlight conceptors as a promising tool for more effective steering of LLMs. Our code is available on github.com/jorispos/conceptorsteering.

papers.title: Using Causal Analysis for Conceptual Deep Learning Explanation
papers.research_question: How to provide clinically relevant explanations for deep learning models in healthcare by associating hidden units with concepts and using causal analysis to ensure influence.
papers.core_contribution: A framework for explaining black-box models using clinically relevant concepts and causal mediation analysis to ensure concepts causally influence the model's decisions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides global explanations for black-box models in terms of clinically relevant concepts that are causally influencing the model's decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Concept classifiers using sparse logistic regression achieve high recall, indicating effective association of hidden units with concepts.
Hidden units act as visual concept detectors, localizing radiographic features without explicit concept supervision during training.
Causal mediation analysis via counterfactual interventions ranks concepts based on indirect effect, with top-ranked concepts being clinically consistent.
The indirect effect is highest in middle layers (dense-block 3), showing their role in mediating decisions.
A decision tree surrogate function provides interpretable global explanations using the top-ranked concepts.
future_direction: Extend concept definition to include a broader set of clinical metrics.

papers.title: FuxiTranyu: A Multilingual Large Language Model Trained with Balanced Data
papers.research_question: How to build a multilingual large language model with balanced data to mitigate performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FuxiTranyu, a multilingual LLM trained on balanced data, which shows competitive performance and more consistent multilingual representations compared to existing models.
papers.conclusion: FuxiTranyu is a strong open-source multilingual LLM, and balanced pre-training data is crucial for achieving consistent multilingual representations and performance.
papers.key_findings:
FuxiTranyu outperforms previous multilingual LLMs like BLOOM-7B1 and PolyLM-13B on several multilingual benchmarks.
Balanced pre-training data leads to more consistent multilingual representations across languages.
Neuron analysis reveals that deep layers are more language-specific and the importance of attention and MLP components varies across layers.
Languages with extremely limited resources (e.g., Bengali, Tamil) are allocated fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model achieves high performance on summarization tasks, outperforming baseline models on XL-Sum.
papers.limitation:
Languages with extremely limited resources, such as Bengali and Tamil, are allocated with fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model underperforms in some tasks (e.g., m-ARC, m-MMLU) due to limited training data for English.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated prowess in a wide range of tasks. However, many LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages. To mitigate this challenge, we present FuxiTranyu, an open-source multilingual LLM, which is designed to satisfy the need of the research community for balanced and high-performing multilingual capabilities. The base model, FuxiTranyu-8B, features 8 billion parameters and is trained from scratch on meticulously balanced multilingual data that contains 600 billion tokens covering 43 natural languages and 16 programming languages. We also develop two instruction-tuned models: FuxiTranyu-8B-SFT which is fine-tuned on a diverse multilingual instruction dataset, and FuxiTranyu-8B-DPO which is further refined with DPO on a preference dataset for enhanced alignment ability. Extensive experiments on a wide range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate the competitive performance of FuxiTranyu against existing multilingual LLMs, e.g., BLOOM-7B, PolyLM-13B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Both neuron and representation interpretability analyses reveal that FuxiTranyu achieves consistent multilingual representations across languages. To promote further research into multilingual LLMs, we release both the base and instruction-tuned FuxiTranyu models together with 58 pre-training checkpoints at HuggingFace (see https://huggingface.co/TJUNLP/FuxiTranyu-8B) and Github (see https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/FuxiTranyu).

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: SAEs Are Good for Steering -- If You Select the Right Features
papers.research_question: How to distinguish between input and output features in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to improve the effectiveness of steering language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a taxonomy of SAE features into input and output types, introduces input and output scores to identify them, and demonstrates that selecting features with high output scores significantly improves steering performance, making unsupervised SAE steering competitive with supervised methods.
papers.conclusion: The work formalizes the roles of SAE features, provides practical scores for feature selection, and shows that output features are key to effective steering, bridging the gap between unsupervised and supervised steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Features in SAEs can be categorized as input features, which capture input patterns, or output features, which influence model outputs.
High input and output scores rarely co-occur in the same features, with input features common in early layers and output features in later layers.
Features with high output scores are more effective for coherent and high-quality steering compared to those with high input scores.
Filtering SAE features based on output scores leads to 2-3x improvements in steering performance on benchmarks like AxBench.
With proper feature selection, SAE steering achieves performance close to supervised methods such as LoRA.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is restricted to features extracted from the residual stream, and does not account for features derived from other components such as attention or MLP layers.
Method focuses on steering using a single SAE feature, ignoring interactions between features that may lead to better effects.
future_direction: Understanding how multiple features combine or interfere for better steering effects.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed as an unsupervised approach to learn a decomposition of a model's latent space. This enables useful applications such as steering - influencing the output of a model towards a desired concept - without requiring labeled data. Current methods identify SAE features to steer by analyzing the input tokens that activate them. However, recent work has highlighted that activations alone do not fully describe the effect of a feature on the model's output. In this work, we draw a distinction between two types of features: input features, which mainly capture patterns in the model's input, and output features, which have a human-understandable effect on the model's output. We propose input and output scores to characterize and locate these types of features, and show that high values for both scores rarely co-occur in the same features. These findings have practical implications: after filtering out features with low output scores, we obtain 2-3x improvements when steering with SAEs, making them competitive with supervised methods.

papers.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improve reconstruction fidelity and interpretability compared to broad-domain SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improves reconstruction fidelity, interpretability, and reduces linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggests the field may need to question 'foundation-model' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Domain-specific SAEs achieve 15-20% higher fraction of variance explained and better loss recovery than broad-domain SAEs.
Domain-specific SAEs produce features that are more interpretable and aligned with clinically meaningful concepts.
Domain-specific SAEs capture more linear structure, leaving a smaller and more nonlinear residual error (less dark matter).
Domain-specific SAEs show improved cosine similarity between activations and reconstructions.
Domain-specific SAEs have minimal shrinkage (relative reconstruction bias close to 1).
future_direction: Extending domain-specific SAEs to other specialised domains, such as legal or financial text.
Investigating how domain confinement affects feature splitting and absorption.
Studying the trade-offs between domain breadth and SAE performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into latent features that reveal mechanistic structure. Conventional SAEs train on broad data distributions, forcing a fixed latent budget to capture only high-frequency, generic patterns. This often results in significant linear ``dark matter'' in reconstruction error and produces latents that fragment or absorb each other, complicating interpretation. We show that restricting SAE training to a well-defined domain (medical text) reallocates capacity to domain-specific features, improving both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability.
