Training JumpReLU SAEs on layer-20 activations of Gemma-2 models using 195k clinical QA examples, we find that domain-confined SAEs explain up to 20\% more variance, achieve higher loss recovery, and reduce linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs. Automated and human evaluations confirm that learned features align with clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., ``taste sensations'' or ``infectious mononucleosis''), rather than frequent but uninformative tokens. These domain-specific SAEs capture relevant linear structure, leaving a smaller, more purely nonlinear residual. We conclude that domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggesting the field may need to question ``foundation-model'' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.

papers.title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for "Quirky" Language Models
papers.research_question: Can internal model features be used to detect anomalous training signals (when models use faulty heuristics) in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Mechanistic anomaly detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks but are not effective across all models and tasks; MAD may be effective in low-stakes applications but requires advances for high-stakes settings.
papers.conclusion: Anomaly detection results are inconsistent across models and tasks; while sometimes highly discriminative, performance degrades to chance in some cases, indicating that more work is needed for reliable real-world application.
papers.key_findings:
Anomaly detector performance varies significantly between models (model-dependent detection).
Detection efficacy is strongly task-dependent (e.g., arithmetic tasks yield higher performance).
Larger deviations in behavior generally make anomalies easier to detect, though not universally.
Anomaly detection performance is closely related to the linear separability of features between normal and anomalous classes.
Detectors that depend on different features (activations vs. attribution) offer somewhat independent signals, but naive combination did not improve performance.
papers.limitation: The manipulations in the datasets are artificial, and real-world tasks will differ systematically, likely with systematic changes in detector performance.
future_direction: Conduct additional experiments to assess whether models trained on more tokens make anomaly detection harder.
Develop benchmarks more closely aligned with intended real-world tasks.
Advances in both detection and evaluation are needed for high-stakes settings.
papers.abstract: As LLMs grow in capability, the task of supervising LLMs becomes more challenging. Supervision failures can occur if LLMs are sensitive to factors that supervisors are unaware of. We investigate Mechanistic Anomaly Detection (MAD) as a technique to augment supervision of capable models; we use internal model features to identify anomalous training signals so they can be investigated or discarded. We train detectors to flag points from the test environment that differ substantially from the training environment, and experiment with a large variety of detector features and scoring rules to detect anomalies in a set of ``quirky'' language models. We find that detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks, but no detector is effective across all models and tasks. MAD techniques may be effective in low-stakes applications, but advances in both detection and evaluation are likely needed if they are to be used in high stakes settings.

papers.title: Group Equivariance Meets Mechanistic Interpretability: Equivariant Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can group symmetries be incorporated into sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, and does this lead to more useful features in downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces adaptively equivariant sparse autoencoders that incorporate group symmetries, which learn features leading to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Adding domain-specific properties like group equivariance to sparse autoencoders can significantly increase their utility in domains beyond language, despite being early results.
papers.key_findings:
A single matrix M can explain more than 98% of the variance in how neural network activations transform under input transformations by a discrete cyclic group.
Equivariant SAEs learn more informative directions in activation space, leading to increased performance on group-structured probing tasks.
Equivariant SAEs lag behind regular SAEs in the reconstruction/sparsity frontier.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to a synthetic task, relatively small models, and a small discrete group.
future_direction: Can M be learned as effectively in larger models such as frontier foundation models?
Can the optimization of M be improved by better utilizing the group structure, e.g., by constraining the optimization to M^|G| = I?
Does the two-layer encoder qualitatively alter what kind of features are discovered, and how can the features best be labeled incorporating the knowledge of how they transform with M?
Can the reconstruction performance of the equivariant SAE be improved to match that of regular SAEs?
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have proven useful in disentangling the opaque activations of neural networks, primarily large language models, into sets of interpretable features. However, adapting them to domains beyond language, such as scientific data with group symmetries, introduces challenges that can hinder their effectiveness. We show that incorporating such group symmetries into the SAEs yields features more useful in downstream tasks. More specifically, we train autoencoders on synthetic images and find that a single matrix can explain how their activations transform as the images are rotated. Building on this, we develop adaptively equivariant SAEs that can adapt to the base model's level of equivariance. These adaptive SAEs discover features that lead to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs, demonstrating the value of incorporating symmetries in mechanistic interpretability tools.

papers.title: Symmetry-Preserving Paths in Integrated Gradients
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether the Integrated Gradients attribution method satisfies completeness and symmetry-preserving properties, and explores its uniqueness among path methods.
papers.core_contribution: Provides rigorous proofs for the completeness and symmetry-preserving properties of Integrated Gradients, and examines its uniqueness among path methods.
papers.conclusion: Integrated Gradients has completeness and symmetry-preserving properties, but it is not uniquely symmetry-preserving among path methods.
papers.key_findings:
Integrated Gradients satisfies completeness and symmetry-preserving properties for Lipschitz continuous functions.
Straight-line paths are IG-symmetry preserving when baseline and input have symmetric variables equal.
IG with straight-line paths is not the unique symmetry-preserving path method, as shown by a counterexample.
papers.limitation: IG with straight-line paths is not the unique symmetry-preserving path method.
papers.abstract: We provide rigorous proofs that the Integrated Gradients (IG) attribution method for deep networks satisfies completeness and symmetry-preserving properties. We also study the uniqueness of IG as a path method preserving symmetry.

papers.title: Discovering symmetry invariants and conserved quantities by interpreting siamese neural networks
papers.research_question: Can Siamese Neural Networks learn symmetry invariants and conserved quantities in physical systems, and can they be interpreted to reveal these quantities without prior knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces interpretable Siamese Neural Networks to theoretical physics and shows they can learn and reveal symmetry invariants and conserved quantities without prior knowledge.
papers.conclusion: SNNs are a useful tool in theoretical physics and can be interpreted to reveal physical invariants, challenging the black box nature of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
SNNs learn the spacetime interval in special relativity.
SNNs learn angular momentum and energy in central potential motion.
SNNs learn the two electromagnetic invariants (E·B and |E|^2-|B|^2).
The bottleneck layer of the SNN can be interpreted via polynomial regression to approximate the invariants.
The SNN fails to learn when the invariant is fixed, indicating it relies on that invariant.
future_direction: Upgrade polynomial regression to symbolic regression.
Combine interpretable SNNs with mathematical reasoning tools (solvers or theorem provers).
Apply to quantum error correction or particle tracking at the LHC.
papers.abstract: The authors train a Siamese neural network to decide whether two different descriptions describe the same physical object. The neural network learns to identify the objects by calculating the underlying invariants and conserved quantities.

papers.title: Beyond the Permutation Symmetry of Transformers: The Role of Rotation for Model Fusion
papers.research_question: How can rotation symmetry in transformers be leveraged to improve model fusion via parameter matching?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces rotation symmetry for transformers, a continuous generalization of permutation symmetry, and proposes a theoretically optimal parameter matching algorithm that improves model fusion by reducing the distance between end models.
papers.conclusion: Rotation symmetry is a valuable extension of parameter space symmetry for transformers, and the proposed parameter matching algorithm effectively enhances model fusion, demonstrating the potential of symmetry for improving deep learning applications.
papers.key_findings:
Rotation symmetry extends the equivalence set of transformers to a continuous space, enabling more flexible and effective parameter matching than discrete permutation symmetry.
The proposed parameter matching algorithm, based on rotation symmetry, significantly reduces the Euclidean distance between end models and improves the performance of various model fusion techniques.
Matching self-attention layers (using rotation symmetry) contributes more to fusion performance in some merging methods (e.g., Fisher, RegMean), while FFN matching (using permutation symmetry) is more beneficial for others (e.g., OTFusion).
Integrating rescaling symmetry with rotation symmetry further refines parameter alignment and leads to additional performance gains.
Matching a subset of layers (particularly the head layers) can achieve most of the performance improvement, offering a trade-off between efficiency and utility.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical optimality guarantee for the parameter matching algorithm is for the two-model case and does not naturally extend to optimal multi-model matching, which remains an open challenge.
The symmetry set considered (rotation, permutation, rescaling) may not be the complete symmetry group of transformers; other structural symmetries may exist.
The sequential optimization of rotation and then rescaling does not guarantee global optimality for the joint optimization over rotation and rescaling parameters.
future_direction: Extending the parameter matching framework to the optimal multi-model setting.
Exploring a richer set of structural symmetries in transformers beyond rotation, permutation, and rescaling.
Developing a joint optimization framework for rotation and rescaling symmetries to achieve global optimality.
papers.abstract: Symmetry in the parameter space of deep neural networks (DNNs) has proven beneficial for various deep learning applications. A well-known example is the permutation symmetry in Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), where permuting the rows of weight matrices in one layer and applying the inverse permutation to adjacent layers yields a functionally equivalent model. While permutation symmetry fully characterizes the equivalence set for MLPs, its discrete nature limits its utility for transformers. In this paper, we introduce rotation symmetry, a novel form of parameter space symmetry for transformers that generalizes permutation symmetry by rotating parameter matrices in self-attention layers. Unlike permutation symmetry, rotation symmetry operates in a continuous domain, thereby significantly expanding the equivalence set for transformers. Based on this property, we propose a theoretically optimal parameter matching algorithm as a plug-and-play module to enhance model fusion. We evaluate our approach using pre-trained transformers across diverse natural language and vision tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our rotation symmetry-based matching algorithm substantially improves model fusion, highlighting the potential of parameter space symmetry to facilitate model fusion. Our code is available on https://github.com/zhengzaiyi/RotationSymmetry.

papers.title: Calibrating LLM Confidence by Probing Perturbed Representation Stability
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM confidence estimation by analyzing the stability of internal representations under targeted adversarial perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CCPS, a method that estimates LLM confidence by analyzing the stability of internal representations under adversarial perturbations, achieving significant improvements in calibration and discrimination metrics across diverse models and benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CCPS provides an efficient, accurate, and generalizable method for LLM confidence estimation, enhancing the trustworthiness of LLMs in critical domains.
papers.key_findings:
CCPS reduces average Expected Calibration Error by approximately 55% (up to 88%) and Brier score by 21% (up to 45%) compared to the best baseline.
CCPS increases average Accuracy by 5 percentage points, AUCPR by 4 percentage points, and AUROC by 6 percentage points.
CCPS generalizes across diverse LLM architectures (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) and model scales (8B to 32B parameters).
CCPS performs well on both multiple-choice and open-ended question answering formats.
CCPS is parameter-efficient, adding only around 9.5k trainable parameters, compared to baselines that may add millions.
papers.abstract: Reza Khanmohammadi, Erfan Miahi, Mehrsa Mardikoraem, Simerjot Kaur, Ivan Brugere, Charese Smiley, Kundan S Thind, Mohammad M. Ghassemi. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: Dynamically Scaled Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be made adaptive so that interventions are applied only when necessary, decoupling when to steer from how to steer?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamically Scaled Activation Steering (DSAS), a method-agnostic framework that adaptively modulates the strength of existing steering methods across layers and inputs, improving the trade-off between desired behavior (e.g., toxicity reduction) and model utility.
papers.conclusion: DSAS is an effective, general framework for conditional activation steering that decouples when to steer from how to steer, consistently improving the trade-off between behavior modification (e.g., toxicity mitigation) and model performance preservation across modalities.
papers.key_findings:
DSAS consistently improves the Pareto front for toxicity mitigation versus capability retention across different steering methods (CAA, ITI, LinEAS) and models (Qwen 2.5, Gemma 2).
DSAS can be trained end-to-end (E2E-DSAS) and matches or outperforms the vanilla DSAS.
DSAS works across modalities (text and image) without modification, enabling concept-specific modulation in text-to-image generation.
DSAS introduces minimal computational overhead and improves interpretability by pinpointing which tokens require steering and by how much.
DSAS outperforms recent conditional steering methods such as CAST and MERA in toxicity mitigation with higher performance retention.
papers.limitation: In image generation, the steering does not precisely localize the target concept spatially.
papers.abstract: Activation steering has emerged as a powerful method for guiding the behavior of generative models towards desired outcomes such as toxicity mitigation. However, most existing methods apply interventions uniformly across all inputs, degrading model performance when steering is unnecessary. We introduce Dynamically Scaled Activation Steering (DSAS), a method-agnostic steering framework that decouples when to steer from how to steer. DSAS adaptively modulates the strength of existing steering transformations across layers and inputs, intervening strongly only when undesired behavior is detected. At generation time, DSAS computes context-dependent scaling factors that selectively adjust the strength of any steering method. We also show how DSAS can be jointly optimized end-to-end together with the steering function. When combined with existing steering methods, DSAS consistently improves the Pareto front with respect to steering alone, achieving a better trade-off between toxicity mitigation and utility preservation. We further demonstrate DSAS's generality by applying it to a text-to-image diffusion model, showing how adaptive steering allows the modulation of specific concepts. Finally, DSAS introduces minimal computational overhead while improving interpretability, pinpointing which tokens require steering and by how much.

papers.title: Extending Activation Steering to Broad Skills and Multiple Behaviours
papers.research_question: Can we extend activation steering to broad skills and multiple behaviours?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can be applied to broad skills (coding) with similar effectiveness as narrow skills, and simultaneous injection of multiple steering vectors at different layers is more promising than combining them into a single vector.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering can be extended to broad skills and multiple behaviours, with simultaneous steering being a promising direction.
papers.key_findings:
Steering to reduce general coding ability is competitive with steering to reduce Python-specific ability.
Individual steering vectors for behaviours like myopia and wealth-seeking are effective.
Combining multiple steering vectors into one vector is largely unsuccessful.
Simultaneous injection of individual steering vectors at different layers is promising and has minor alignment tax.
Steering at layer 0 for coding ability had an opposite effect, possibly due to copy suppression.
papers.limitation:
The flexibility of activation steering makes finding optimal setups non-trivial.
It is unclear whether reductions in matching scores (e.g., a 20% reduction in coding accuracy) translate to real-world risk reduction.
future_direction: Testing with other models to understand the general working of activation steering.
Using different injection coefficients for different steering vectors in simultaneous steering.
Generating and injecting steering vectors at different places within a layer (e.g., attention and MLP components).
Steering against alternative programming languages to further investigate broad steering.
papers.abstract: Current large language models have dangerous capabilities, which are likely to become more problematic in the future. Activation steering techniques can be used to reduce risks from these capabilities. In this paper, we investigate the efficacy of activation steering for broad skills and multiple behaviours. First, by comparing the effects of reducing performance on general coding ability and Python-specific ability, we find that steering broader skills is competitive to steering narrower skills. Second, we steer models to become more or less myopic and wealth-seeking, among other behaviours. In our experiments, combining steering vectors for multiple different behaviours into one steering vector is largely unsuccessful. On the other hand, injecting individual steering vectors at different places in a model simultaneously is promising.

papers.title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations
papers.research_question: How do cognitive and expressive capabilities develop and interact in large language models across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback stages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cognitive capabilities in LLMs are established during pretraining, while expressive capabilities develop during SFT and RLHF, with cognitive capability setting an upper bound for expressive capability.
papers.conclusion: This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of LLM training processes.
papers.key_findings:
Cognitive capability is primarily established during the pretraining stage, whereas expressive capability develops during SFT and RLHF.
There is a strong statistical correlation between cognitive and expressive capabilities, with cognitive capability acting as an upper bound.
The gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities can be bridged by optimization-free methods such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling.
The vocabulary linear layer plays a crucial role in expressive capability, and its training during SFT/RLHF helps reduce the gap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals a plateau in cognitive capability in deeper layers, indicating redundancy in the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring additional linear analysis techniques for model analysis and control.
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model's cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model's capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs' architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

papers.title: On Hierarchical Encoding and Reasoning in Deep Transformer-based Generative Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internalize hierarchical structures from data, what is the relationship between this internalization and behaviors like generalization versus memorization, and how can insights into hierarchical reasoning guide the development of more unified, robust, and interpretable multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis investigates how Transformer models learn and represent hierarchical structures, develops methods to probe these structures and mitigate harmful memorization, introduces the PSViT model for hierarchical video prediction, and demonstrates a unified next-frame prediction framework for multimodal tasks.
papers.conclusion: The capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional Transformer models (e.g., BERT) concentrate hierarchical linguistic information near the top layers, while autoregressive/permutation-masked models (e.g., GPT-2, XLNet, Reformer) distribute it more evenly.
Verbatim memorization during fine-tuning is often preceded by a spike in n-gram overlap, which can be used for early-stopping or regularization to reduce leakage by up to 90%.
The PSViT model, designed with hierarchical priors, outperforms latent-space baselines on physical simulation benchmarks, extending accurate prediction horizons by up to 50%.
Abstract physical parameters governing video dynamics are most linearly recoverable from the middle layers of PSViT, mirroring the mid-layer abstraction peak for linguistic hierarchy.
Diverse tasks across text, image, audio, and video can be reformulated into a unified next-frame prediction task, enabling a single PSViT-based model to achieve competitive performance without modality-specific encoders.
papers.limitation:
Probing tasks relied primarily on English datasets (SST, PTB), limiting linguistic diversity.
Memorization experiments used datasets of up to 5,000 samples and greedy decoding; different scales or decoding strategies may alter dynamics.
PSViT was evaluated at 128x128 resolution on deterministic simulations; generalizability to complex real-world video is untested.
The multimodal model was trained separately per task; joint multitask training might better foster shared representations.
future_direction: Extend ancestor probing to morphologically rich languages, different syntactic formalisms, and broader discourse structures.
Scale the n-gram-aware loss regularizer to operate efficiently on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Test PSViT on larger-scale, stochastic, real-world video and integrate differentiable renderers for more direct interpretability.
Explore joint multitask training on a diverse corpus of reformulated multimodal data and richer encodings within the visual canvas.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative Transformer-based foundation models have driven remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, yet their internal mechanisms for representing complex hierarchical structures remain largely unknown, posing significant challenges for interpretability, safety, and robust generalisation. This thesis aims to progress on these issues by systematically investigating how such models internalise hierarchical structures, the relationship between this learning and behaviours like generalisation versus memorisation, and how hierarchical principles can inform the development of safer, more accurate, generative models. To this end, we first introduce novel probing techniques to map the layer-wise emergence of linguistic hierarchies in language models and extend this analysis to the visual domain by developing PSViT: a pixel-space Transformer with hierarchical decompositions of video image patches, shown to learn and generalise hierarchical physical dynamics from raw video data. We investigate memorisation during fine-tuning, establishing an n-gram based early warning signal for verbatim leakage and proposing scalable defences that promote structural generalisation over verbatim memorisation. Building on these insights, we further demonstrate that a unified next-frame prediction framework enables a single model to process text, images, audio, and video without modality-specific encoders, thereby learning shared hierarchical patterns across these diverse inputs. Collectively, our findings underscore that the capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and that a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Thinking Language Models via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: Can reasoning behaviors in thinking language models be controlled using steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that reasoning behaviors in thinking LLMs are mediated by linear directions in the activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors extracted via difference of means and attribution patching.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a practical method for controlling reasoning behaviors in thinking models, opening new possibilities for fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Thinking models exhibit distinct reasoning behaviors such as backtracking, uncertainty estimation, and example testing.
These behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space.
Steering vectors extracted via difference of means can control these behaviors, increasing or decreasing their occurrence.
The steering approach works across different model architectures within the DeepSeek-R1-Distill family.
The method provides a practical tool for modulating reasoning capabilities in thinking models.
papers.limitation:
The automated annotation process using GPT-4o has occasionally produced false positives and false negatives in identifying reasoning patterns.
The generalization of these findings to other models that have undergone reward-based RL training instead of being fine-tuned on thinking models remains an open question.
future_direction: Developing more robust annotation methods, potentially incorporating multiple models or human validation.
Extending the research to a broader range of models to understand the universality of thinking mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to the development of thinking language models that generate extensive internal reasoning chains before producing responses. While these models achieve improved performance, controlling their reasoning processes remains challenging. This work presents a steering approach for thinking LLMs by analyzing and manipulating specific reasoning behaviors in DeepSeek-R1-Distill models. Through a systematic experiment on 500 tasks across 10 diverse categories, we identify several reasoning behaviors exhibited by thinking models, including expressing uncertainty, generating examples for hypothesis validation, and backtracking in reasoning chains. We demonstrate that these behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors. By extracting and applying these vectors, we provide a method to modulate specific aspects of the model's reasoning process, such as its tendency to backtrack or express uncertainty. Our approach offers practical tools for steering reasoning processes in thinking models in a controlled and interpretable manner. We validate our steering method using three DeepSeek-R1-Distill models, demonstrating consistent control across different model architectures.

papers.title: Learning local discrete features in explainable-by-design convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we design a convolutional neural network that is both high-performance and explainable by using a lateral inhibition mechanism to learn local discrete features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ExplaiNet, an explainable-by-design CNN that uses a lateral inhibition layer to learn local discrete feature vectors, enabling high accuracy and providing explanations via a probabilistic graph and motif discovery.
papers.conclusion: The ExplaiNet framework breaks the performance-explainability trade-off by introducing an explainable-by-design CNN that retains or surpasses baseline performance while providing causal explanations based on discrete feature motifs.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed ExplaiNet model achieves comparable or better performance than baseline ResNet and DenseNet architectures on tiny image datasets while providing explanations.
The lateral inhibition layer amplifies gradients of winner neurons, leading to ordered activations and the formation of local discrete feature vectors.
Feature motif discovery using the EXTREME algorithm reduces the vocabulary of local discrete features, providing concise explanations.
The explainer probabilistic graph can infer causal relationships between motifs of adjacent levels and attribute the model's output to global motifs.
Experiments show that the explainer can sometimes correctly classify samples that the neural predictor misclassifies, suggesting potential for ensemble use or adversarial sample detection.
papers.limitation:
Further research on regularization aspects of the lateral inhibition function is required to investigate the magnitude of weights and activations during training.
Experiments are limited to tiny image datasets due to computational resources; the method has not been tested on medium-resolution images or high numbers of classes.
future_direction: Investigate the proper amount of weight decay and restriction of input values for positively monotonic gradient amplification in the lateral inhibition function.
Scale up the method to train models on medium-resolution images, high number of classes, and with millions of parameters.
Adjust the EXTREME algorithm to support custom numeric system bases, making the conversion to the quaternary system optional.
papers.abstract: Our proposed framework attempts to break the trade-off between performance and explainability by introducing an explainable-by-design convolutional neural network (CNN) based on the lateral inhibition mechanism. The ExplaiNet model consists of the predictor, that is a high-accuracy CNN with residual or dense skip connections, and the explainer probabilistic graph that expresses the spatial interactions of the network neurons. The value on each graph node is a local discrete feature (LDF) vector, a patch descriptor that represents the indices of antagonistic neurons ordered by the strength of their activations, which are learned with gradient descent. Using LDFs as sequences we can increase the conciseness of explanations by repurposing EXTREME, an EM-based sequence motif discovery method that is typically used in molecular biology. Having a discrete feature motif matrix for each one of intermediate image representations, instead of a continuous activation tensor, allows us to leverage the inherent explainability of Bayesian networks. By collecting observations and directly calculating probabilities, we can explain causal relationships between motifs of adjacent levels and attribute the model's output to global motifs. Moreover, experiments on various tiny image benchmark datasets confirm that our predictor ensures the same level of performance as the baseline architecture for a given count of parameters and/or layers. Our novel method shows promise to exceed this performance while providing an additional stream of explanations. In the solved MNIST classification task, it reaches a comparable to the state-of-the-art performance for single models, using standard training setup and 0.75 million parameters.

papers.title: Theoretical Analysis of Positional Encodings in Transformer Models: Impact on Expressiveness and Generalization
papers.research_question: What classes of sequence-to-sequence functions can a transformer approximate under different positional encoding schemes? How do positional encodings affect a transformer's ability to generalize and extrapolate to sequences longer than those seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: Presents a unified theoretical framework for analyzing positional encodings in transformers, deriving expressiveness definitions, generalization bounds, and extrapolation analyses, and proposes novel orthogonal function-based encoding schemes.
papers.conclusion: Positional encodings fundamentally shape a transformer's capabilities. The theoretical framework, combined with novel PE schemes and lightweight validation, lays the groundwork for more robust, generalizable, and extrapolatable transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
All common positional encodings yield universal approximation for fixed-length sequences, with ALiBi extending universality to arbitrary lengths.
Generalization bounds for transformer classes depend on input norm bounds; normalized wavelet and Legendre encodings match sinusoidal PEs.
ALiBi's linear bias ensures graceful extrapolation up to a factor of c*N_max, with error growing linearly in distance beyond training length.
Wavelet-based encodings exhibit exponential decay in encoding differences beyond N_max, ensuring strong extrapolation.
Lightweight experiments on a synthetic running-sum task show wavelet-based encodings outperform other methods when extrapolating to 4x training length.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on transformer encoders without layer normalization, dropout, or multi-head complexities; including these may affect Lipschitz constants and generalization.
Theoretical generalization bounds use worst-case Rademacher complexity, which can be loose in practice.
Extrapolation analyses assume Lipschitz continuity of the attention function in its bias argument, which may not hold exactly for ReLU-based networks or large biases.
Experiments use a minimal transformer on a synthetic task; real-world benchmarks may reveal additional behaviors.
future_direction: Extend expressiveness and generalization analyses to multi-head settings, accounting for head interactions and layer normalization.
Investigate methods to adapt ALiBi's slope dynamically based on sequence length or task.
Explore other orthogonal function families tailored for specific domains (e.g., vision sequences, time-series).
Benchmark wavelet and Legendre encodings on real-world tasks that require long-context reasoning.
Extend the information-theoretic perspective to quantify how much positional mutual information is transferred across layers.
papers.abstract: Positional encodings are a core part of transformer-based models, enabling processing of sequential data without recurrence. This paper presents a theoretical framework to analyze how various positional encoding methods, including sinusoidal, learned, relative, and bias-based methods like Attention with Linear Biases (ALiBi), impact a transformer's expressiveness, generalization ability, and extrapolation to longer sequences. Expressiveness is defined via function approximation, generalization bounds are established using Rademacher complexity, and new encoding methods based on orthogonal functions, such as wavelets and Legendre polynomials, are proposed. The extrapolation capacity of existing and proposed encodings is analyzed, extending ALiBi's biasing approach to a unified theoretical context. Experimental evaluation on synthetic sequence-to-sequence tasks shows that orthogonal transform-based encodings outperform traditional sinusoidal encodings in generalization and extrapolation. This work addresses a critical gap in transformer theory, providing insights for design choices in natural language processing, computer vision, and other transformer applications.

papers.title: Beyond Interpretability: The Gains of Feature Monosemanticity on Model Robustness
papers.research_question: Does feature monosemanticity, which improves interpretability, also improve model robustness, challenging the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff?
papers.core_contribution: This paper challenges the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff by showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also provide concrete gains in model robustness across various scenarios including noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that monosemanticity offers advantages beyond interpretability, improving model robustness across multiple learning scenarios, and advocates for exploring its broader learning benefits.
papers.key_findings:
Monosemantic features (from NCL or SAE) are more robust than polysemantic features under linear probing with label noise and input noise.
Maintaining monosemanticity during finetuning (via non-negative tuning) reduces overfitting and improves performance in few-shot and noisy-label settings.
MonoLoRA, a sparse variant of LoRA, better preserves alignment safety while maintaining task performance when finetuning LLMs on small datasets.
Empirical analysis shows that classifiers with higher robustness under noise rely more on monosemantic features.
Theoretical analysis on a toy model indicates monosemantic features have better linear separability under noise, leading to more robust decision boundaries.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models often suffer from a lack of interpretability due to polysemanticity, where individual neurons are activated by multiple unrelated semantics, resulting in unclear attributions of model behavior. Recent advances in monosemanticity, where neurons correspond to consistent and distinct semantics, have significantly improved interpretability but are commonly believed to compromise accuracy. In this work, we challenge the prevailing belief of the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff, showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also bring concrete gains in model performance. Across multiple robust learning scenarios-including input and label noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization-our results show that models leveraging monosemantic features significantly outperform those relying on polysemantic features. Furthermore, we provide empirical and theoretical understandings on the robustness gains of feature monosemanticity. Our preliminary analysis suggests that monosemanticity, by promoting better separation of feature representations, leads to more robust decision boundaries. This diverse evidence highlights the generality of monosemanticity in improving model robustness. As a first step in this new direction, we embark on exploring the learning benefits of monosemanticity beyond interpretability, supporting the long-standing hypothesis of linking interpretability and robustness. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/PKU-ML/Beyond_Interpretability}.

papers.title: Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness of Language Models
papers.research_question: Can language models internally distinguish between testing and deployment phases (evaluation awareness), and how can this capability be probed and steered?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that evaluation awareness is linearly represented in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and can be extracted using linear probes, and that steering with evaluation-awareness-relevant SAE features can partially uncover sandbagging behavior.
papers.conclusion: Modern language models develop internal representations that distinguish evaluation from deployment contexts; current evaluation scenarios may be readily identifiable as artificial, highlighting the need for more realistic evaluation frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes trained on model activations can detect evaluation contexts with high AUROC scores (up to 0.829).
The probes generalize across different evaluation and deployment prompt datasets.
Current safety evaluation prompts (e.g., for deception) are often classified as test-like, suggesting models may recognize them as artificial evaluations.
Steering with SAE features related to evaluation awareness can partially recover sandbagged capabilities on the WMDP benchmark, but linear probe steering had minimal impact.
Evaluation awareness representations are more distinctly encoded in earlier model layers (e.g., layers 23-24).
papers.limitation:
The evaluation awareness observed in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct may be less pronounced than in frontier models, raising concerns about generalizability.
Linear probes may not capture the full complexity of evaluation awareness, which may not be strictly one-dimensionally linear.
The experimental setup is a significant simplification compared to real-world scenarios of concern (e.g., extended agentic backdoor honeypots).
Steering attempts using linear probes and SAE features showed limited success in modifying sandbagging behavior.
future_direction: Comprehensive red-teaming with alternative probe training methods (e.g., logistic regression, PCA, non-linear probes).
Leveraging probes to enhance the realism of scheming honeypots via automated prompt authenticity enhancement.
Integrating probe-based detection into control protocols as a low-latency whitebox monitoring system.
papers.abstract: Language models can distinguish between testing and deployment phases -- a capability known as evaluation awareness. This has significant safety and policy implications, potentially undermining the reliability of evaluations that are central to AI governance frameworks and voluntary industry commitments. In this paper, we study evaluation awareness in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. We show that linear probes can separate real-world evaluation and deployment prompts, suggesting that current models internally represent this distinction. We also find that current safety evaluations are correctly classified by the probes, suggesting that they already appear artificial or inauthentic to models. Our findings underscore the importance of ensuring trustworthy evaluations and understanding deceptive capabilities. More broadly, our work showcases how model internals may be leveraged to support blackbox methods in safety audits, especially for future models more competent at evaluation awareness and deception.

papers.title: Multi-scale Graph Autoregressive Modeling: Molecular Property Prediction via Next Token Prediction
papers.research_question: How can we bridge the gap between graph topology preservation and scalable autoregressive training to enable decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Connection-Aware Motif Sequencing (CamS), a graph-to-sequence representation that enables decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via next-token prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance on molecular property prediction benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CamS bridges the gap between graph topology and autoregressive training, enabling effective molecular property prediction via next-token prediction with a standard decoder-only Transformer backbone.
papers.key_findings:
CamS-LLaMA achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoleculeNet and MoleculeACE benchmarks.
Multi-scale concatenation is the key driver of performance.
The causal serialization effectively drives attention toward cliff-determining structural differences.
CamS provides a more nuanced structural discrimination than descriptor-based approaches like KPGT.
The method combines general-purpose robustness with fine-grained structural discriminability.
papers.limitation: Vocabulary materialization involves expensive subgraph-isomorphism matching that prohibits direct training on billion-scale corpora.
papers.abstract: We present Connection-Aware Motif Sequencing (CamS), a graph-to-sequence representation that enables decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via standard next-token prediction (NTP). For molecular property prediction, SMILES-based NTP scales well but lacks explicit topology, whereas graph-native masked modeling captures connectivity but risks disrupting the pivotal chemical details (e.g., activity cliffs). CamS bridges this gap by serializing molecular graphs into structure-rich causal sequences. CamS first mines data-driven connection-aware motifs. It then serializes motifs via scaffold-rooted breadth-first search (BFS) to establish a stable core-to-periphery order. Crucially, CamS enables hierarchical modeling by concatenating sequences from fine to coarse motif scales, allowing the model to condition global scaffolds on dense, uncorrupted local structural evidence. We instantiate CamS-LLaMA by pre-training a vanilla LLaMA backbone on CamS sequences. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoleculeNet and the activity-cliff benchmark MoleculeACE, outperforming both SMILES-based language models and strong graph baselines. Interpretability analysis confirms that our multi-scale causal serialization effectively drives attention toward cliff-determining differences.

papers.title: Position: Mechanistic Interpretability Should Prioritize Feature Consistency in SAEs
papers.research_question: How can feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be achieved and measured to improve the reliability of mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and proposes the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to measure consistency. It shows that high consistency is achievable with appropriate architectural choices (e.g., TopK SAEs) and that high PW-MCC correlates with semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.conclusion: The paper calls for a community-wide shift towards valuing and systematically measuring feature consistency in SAEs for cumulative progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
High feature consistency (PW-MCC ≈ 0.80) is achievable with TopK SAEs on real-world LLM activations.
PW-MCC reliably tracks ground-truth feature recovery (GT-MCC) in synthetic experiments.
Feature consistency is frequency-dependent: more frequent features are learned more consistently.
Different SAE architectures yield different levels of consistency, with TopK SAEs performing best.
High PW-MCC scores correlate strongly with the semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.limitation:
The focus is on SAEs, and other interpretability methods may have different consistency challenges.
The study uses a specific metric (PW-MCC) for a specific notion of consistency (strong feature consistency).
The real-world experiments are limited to two base models and one dataset.
The automated interpretation pipeline has its own limitations.
future_direction: Extending consistency analysis to other interpretability methods beyond SAEs.
Developing more nuanced metrics for consistency that go beyond strong feature consistency.
Investigating the relationship between consistency and downstream task performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a prominent tool in mechanistic interpretability (MI) for decomposing neural network activations into interpretable features. However, the aspiration to identify a canonical set of features is challenged by the observed inconsistency of learned SAE features across different training runs, undermining the reliability and efficiency of MI research. This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in SAEs -- the reliable convergence to equivalent feature sets across independent runs. We propose using the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to operationalize consistency and demonstrate that high levels are achievable (0.80 for TopK SAEs on LLM activations) with appropriate architectural choices. Our contributions include detailing the benefits of prioritizing consistency; providing theoretical grounding and synthetic validation using a model organism, which verifies PW-MCC as a reliable proxy for ground-truth recovery; and extending these findings to real-world LLM data, where high feature consistency strongly correlates with the semantic similarity of learned feature explanations. We call for a community-wide shift towards systematically measuring feature consistency to foster robust cumulative progress in MI.

papers.title: Discovering the Compositional Structure of Vector Representations with Role Learning Networks
papers.research_question: How can neural networks perform so well on compositional tasks even though they lack explicit compositional representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ROLE, a method that learns to approximate neural network encodings with compositional symbolic structures, and shows that RNNs trained on the fully-compositional SCAN task learn such structures.
papers.conclusion: ROLE can discover latent symbolic structure in RNNs trained on fully-compositional tasks, but sentence embeddings from models trained on partially-compositional tasks show little evidence of such structure.
papers.key_findings:
ROLE approximates the encodings of a GRU RNN on the SCAN task with 94.83% substitution accuracy, indicating the RNN learned compositional representations.
The learned role scheme can be interpreted as a symbolic algorithm that assigns roles based on position and context within the input sequence.
The discovered compositional structure is causally relevant: surgically replacing constituents in the encoding based on the symbolic structure changes the model's output as predicted.
For sentence embedding models (InferSent, Skip-thought, SST, SPINN) trained on partially-compositional tasks, ROLE finds little evidence that their encodings possess compositional structure.
The paper provides a closed-form equation for the SCAN encoder's embeddings as a sum of tensor products of filler and role vectors.
papers.limitation:
ROLE requires single-vector sentence representations, making it difficult to apply to Transformer architectures which typically use variable-sized collections of vectors.
It is still unknown how the weights in the neural network actually convert the raw input into a Tensor Product Representation.
future_direction: Applying ROLE to representations of partial sequences to study how TPRs are built incrementally.
Applying ROLE to Transformer architectures to discover compositional structure.
Using ROLE to suggest inductive biases for improving models' generalization on partially-compositional datasets.
papers.abstract: How can neural networks perform so well on compositional tasks even though they lack explicit compositional representations? We use a novel analysis technique called ROLE to show that recurrent neural networks perform well on such tasks by converging to solutions which implicitly represent symbolic structure. This method uncovers a symbolic structure which, when properly embedded in vector space, closely approximates the encodings of a standard seq2seq network trained to perform the compositional SCAN task. We verify the causal importance of the discovered symbolic structure by showing that, when we systematically manipulate hidden embeddings based on this symbolic structure, the model's output is changed in the way predicted by our analysis.

papers.title: Can sparse autoencoders be used to decompose and interpret steering vectors?
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why directly applying sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two main reasons why sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide misleading decompositions of steering vectors: (1) steering vectors are out-of-distribution for SAEs, and (2) SAEs cannot represent negative coefficients which are meaningful in steering vectors.
papers.conclusion: Direct SAE decomposition of steering vectors is misleading due to out-of-distribution and non-negativity constraints; alternative approaches such as learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors have significantly smaller L2-norms than model activations, causing the SAE encoder bias to dominate the decomposition and yield misleading results.
Scaling steering vectors does not resolve the out-of-distribution issue because steering vectors lack default components present in model activations.
SAEs restrict decompositions to non-negative coefficients, but steering vectors have meaningful negative projections in feature directions.
Negative projections in steering vectors can cause spurious positive activations in SAE features due to negative cosine similarities between features.
These issues explain prior observations of irrelevant features in SAE decompositions and the failure of SAE-reconstructed vectors to retain steering properties.
papers.limitation:
The proposed alternative method of learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis requires two SAE decompositions per difference vector, increasing the potential impact of SAE error.
The corrigibility steering vectors may include confounding features related to computer science and language modeling.
future_direction: Explore learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis and establish evaluation metrics to compare with alternative methods.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a promising approach to control the behaviour of large language models. However, their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) may offer a potential method to interpret steering vectors, recent findings show that SAE-reconstructed vectors often lack the steering properties of the original vectors. This paper investigates why directly applying SAEs to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions, identifying two reasons: (1) steering vectors fall outside the input distribution for which SAEs are designed, and (2) steering vectors can have meaningful negative projections in feature directions, which SAEs are not designed to accommodate. These limitations hinder the direct use of SAEs for interpreting steering vectors.

papers.title: Patterning: The Dual of Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the dual problem to interpretability? The paper introduces patterning as the dual: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data leads to it.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces patterning as the dual of interpretability, using susceptibilities to derive data interventions that steer internal structure formation in neural networks, demonstrated in small language models and a synthetic task.
papers.conclusion: Patterning provides a principled approach to steering generalization by inverting the susceptibility relationship, with potential applications to AI alignment and control of internal structure.
papers.key_findings:
Re-weighting training data along the second principal susceptibility direction can accelerate or delay the formation of the induction circuit.
In the parentheses balancing task, patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution.
Susceptibility-guided interventions produce predictable changes in internal structures.
papers.limitation:
Experiments use small models (3M parameters) and simple tasks.
Susceptibility estimation is computationally expensive.
Focus on one-off interventions made at the start of training, not online control.
Theoretical framework assumes infinitesimal perturbations, while practical interventions are finite; understanding when the linear approximation breaks down is important.
Connection between observables and downstream behavior (e.g., safety properties) requires further study.
future_direction: Develop online control (adjusting data distribution dynamically during training).
Scale to larger models and more efficient methods.
Study the connection to safety properties and AI alignment applications.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how neural networks generalize beyond their training data by reverse-engineering their internal structures. We introduce patterning as the dual problem: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data produces it. Our approach is based on susceptibilities, which measure how posterior expectation values of observables respond to infinitesimal shifts in the data distribution. Inverting this linear response relationship yields the data intervention that steers the model toward a target internal configuration. We demonstrate patterning in a small language model, showing that re-weighting training data along principal susceptibility directions can accelerate or delay the formation of structure, such as the induction circuit. In a synthetic parentheses balancing task where multiple algorithms achieve perfect training accuracy, we show that patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution. These results establish that the same mathematical framework used to read internal structure can be inverted to write it.

papers.title: Dy-mer: An Explainable DNA Sequence Representation Scheme using Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How to create an interpretable and robust DNA sequence representation scheme that captures local subsequence features and improves generalization on small datasets?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Dy-mer, an interpretable DNA representation scheme based on dictionary learning that formulates an optimization problem in tensor format, learns a dymer dictionary and sparse representations, and achieves state-of-the-art performance in downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Dy-mer provides a transparent and effective framework for DNA sequence representation, enabling both high predictive performance and interpretability for biological applications.
papers.key_findings:
Dy-mer outperforms existing methods in DNA promoter classification with at least 14% improvement in accuracy.
The learned dymers match known DNA motifs such as GC-rich regions, TATA box, and CCAAT box.
Clustering using Dy-mer yields semantically meaningful phylogenetic trees that align with biological taxonomy.
The method demonstrates robustness and interpretability, making it suitable for biological research.
future_direction: Explore the application of the representation scheme on more biological tasks.
papers.abstract: DNA sequences encode critical genetic information, yet their variable length and discrete nature impede direct utilization in deep learning models. Existing DNA representation schemes convert sequences into numerical vectors but fail to capture structural features of local subsequences and often suffer from limited interpretability and poor generalization on small datasets. To address these limitations, we propose Dy-mer, an interpretable and robust DNA representation scheme based on dictionary learning. Dy-mer formulates an optimization problem in tensor format, which ensures computational efficiency in batch processing. Our scheme reconstructs DNA sequences as concatenations of dynamic-length subsequences (dymers) through a convolution operation and simultaneously optimize a learnable dymer dictionary and sparse representations. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in downstream tasks such as DNA promoter classification and motif detection. Experiments further show that the learned dymers match known DNA motifs and clustering using Dy-mer yields semantically meaningful phylogenetic trees. These results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves both strong predictive performance and high interpretability, making it well suited for biological research applications.

papers.title: Interpreting and Controlling LLM Reasoning through Integrated Policy Gradient
papers.research_question: How can we identify and control internal components in LLMs that contribute sequentially to reasoning behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Integrated Policy Gradient (IPG), a training-free framework that attributes reasoning behaviors to internal components using outcome-oriented signals and enables precise control of reasoning capabilities.
papers.conclusion: IPG provides a robust framework for interpreting and controlling reasoning in LLMs, improving transparency and controllability of internal mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
IPG identifies internal components with sequential influence on reasoning behaviors, enabling effective enhancement and suppression of accuracy across datasets.
IPG allows fine-grained control over reasoning behaviors such as capability and strength by modulating identified components.
Components identified by IPG show transferability across different model variants within the same family.
IPG provides interpretability over specific reasoning aspects like problem understanding and task decomposition.
IPG outperforms existing methods like text-pattern and control-vector approaches in localization and control effectiveness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong reasoning abilities in solving complex real-world problems. Yet, the internal mechanisms driving these complex reasoning behaviors remain opaque. Existing interpretability approaches targeting reasoning either identify components (e.g., neurons) correlated with special textual patterns, or rely on human-annotated contrastive pairs to derive control vectors. Consequently, current methods struggle to precisely localize complex reasoning mechanisms or capture sequential influence from model internal workings to the reasoning outputs. In this paper, built on outcome-oriented and sequential-influence-aware principles, we focus on identifying components that have sequential contribution to reasoning behavior where outcomes are cumulated by long-range effects. We propose Integrated Policy Gradient (IPG), a novel framework that attributes reasoning behaviors to model's inner components by propagating compound outcome-based signals such as post reasoning accuracy backward through model inference trajectories. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our approach achieves more precise localization and enables reliable modulation of reasoning behaviors (e.g., reasoning capability, reasoning strength) across diverse reasoning models.

papers.title: Learning a Fourier Transform for Linear Relative Positional Encodings in Transformers
papers.research_question: How to efficiently incorporate a wide range of relative positional encoding mechanisms (RPEs) into linear Transformers, enabling linear complexity for both sequential and geometric data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FourierLearner-Transformers (FLTs), a class of linear Transformers that efficiently incorporate relative positional encodings (RPEs) by learning their spectral representation, achieving linear complexity and applicability to sequential and geometric data.
papers.conclusion: FLTs provide an efficient and effective method for incorporating RPEs into linear attention Transformers, with theoretical approximation guarantees and strong empirical performance across text, image, and 3D molecular data.
papers.key_findings:
FLTs outperform other linear Transformers (e.g., Performer, CosFormer) on language modeling (WikiText-103) by achieving lower perplexity.
FLTs achieve higher accuracy than baselines on image classification tasks (ImageNet, Places365, Fashion-MNIST).
For 3D molecular property prediction (OC20 dataset), FLTs with RPEs provide better energy prediction accuracy (lower MAE, higher EwT) than Performers without RPEs.
FLTs maintain linear time and space complexity, being more memory-efficient than log-linear Performer baselines.
FLTs can learn local RPEs and exhibit both local and global attention patterns in language modeling.
papers.abstract: We propose a new class of linear Transformers called FourierLearner-Transformers (FLTs), which incorporate a wide range of relative positional encoding mechanisms (RPEs). These include regular RPE techniques applied for sequential data, as well as novel RPEs operating on geometric data embedded in higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces. FLTs construct the optimal RPE mechanism implicitly by learning its spectral representation. As opposed to other architectures combining efficient low-rank linear attention with RPEs, FLTs remain practical in terms of their memory usage and do not require additional assumptions about the structure of the RPE mask. Besides, FLTs allow for applying certain structural inductive bias techniques to specify masking strategies, e.g. they provide a way to learn the so-called local RPEs introduced in this paper and give accuracy gains as compared with several other linear Transformers for language modeling. We also thoroughly test FLTs on other data modalities and tasks, such as image classification, 3D molecular modeling, and learnable optimizers. To the best of our knowledge, for 3D molecular data, FLTs are the first Transformer architectures providing linear attention and incorporating RPE masking.

papers.title: Integrating Evolutionary and Compositional Features with ML and DL for Robust and Interpretable Druggable Protein Prediction
papers.research_question: How can evolutionary and compositional features be integrated with machine learning and deep learning for robust and interpretable druggable protein prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a hybrid feature representation combining Average Block-based PSSM and Dipeptide Composition for druggable protein prediction, achieving high accuracy with statistical validation and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The hybrid feature representation enables strong predictive performance for druggable protein prediction, with SVM and CapsBiLSTM achieving high accuracy and AUC scores, validated statistically, and providing interpretable insights into sequence descriptors.
papers.key_findings:
Hybrid features (AB-PSSM + DPC) significantly outperform individual descriptors in predicting druggable proteins.
SVM and CapsBiLSTM models achieve classification accuracies above 90% and ROC-AUC/PR-AUC scores above 95%.
Statistical tests (DeLong's test, McNemar's test, bootstrap confidence intervals) confirm the robustness and significance of the improvements.
Interpretability analyses using SHAP and t-SNE reveal biologically significant sequence descriptors influencing druggability.
The proposed framework outperforms existing machine learning and ensemble-based methods in accuracy and interpretability.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Druggable proteins are essential targets in contemporary therapeutic discovery, and their precise identification is necessary for the progression of rational drug design. Traditional biochemical screening techniques are costly, laborious, and protracted, whereas current computational models typically attain only moderate efficacy and seldom offer robust statistical validation or biological interpretability. To mitigate these limitations, we offer a hybrid computational approach that amalgamates evolutionary and compositional information by merging Average Block-based Position-Specific Scoring Matrix (AB-PSSM) characteristics with Dipeptide Composition (DPC) into a 600-dimensional representation. The hybrid feature space was assessed utilizing three machine learning algorithms (support vector machine, random forest, and XGBoost) alongside three deep learning architectures (CapsBiLSTM, ResCapsNetPlus, and ResNet1D) following a rigorous five-fold out-of-fold cross-validation protocol to guarantee fairness and reproducibility. A thorough assessment revealed that the hybrid attributes significantly surpassed individual descriptors, with the SVM and CapsBiLSTM classifiers attaining classification accuracies of 90% and ROC-AUC and PR-AUC values surpassing 95%. The robustness and reliability were further validated by statistical analyses, including DeLong’s test, McNemar’s test, and bootstrap confidence intervals, demonstrating that the observed enhancements were substantial and consistent. Furthermore, interpretability investigations employing SHAP feature attribution and t-SNE visualization underscored biologically significant sequence descriptors as pivotal factors influencing druggability, thus mitigating the "black box" constraint inherent in numerous deep learning methodologies. This study presents a statistically validated, interpretable, and high-performing framework for predicting druggable proteins, which outperforms current machine learning and ensemble-based methods, establishing a clear basis for future applications in precision medicine and drug discovery.

papers.title: DISCO: Disentangled Communication Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Is steering the query and value representation spaces within attention heads more effective for controlling LLM behavior than steering attention head outputs or other spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISCO Steering, a method that injects steering vectors directly into the query and value spaces of attention heads, providing more granular control and superior performance over existing steering vector baselines.
papers.conclusion: Query and value spaces are powerful building blocks for steering vector methods, and DISCO provides an effective and flexible approach for controlling LLM behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Query and value spaces exhibit higher linear discriminability of concepts compared to attention head outputs.
DISCO Steering disentangles the strong Communication Steering baseline, allowing independent control of query and value steering magnitudes.
DISCO achieves the best performance in 13 out of 16 experiments across multiple datasets and models.
Steering query spaces dynamically re-weights attention, while steering value spaces directly adds to the head output.
The method is effective for promoting and suppressing behaviors like truthfulness, power-seeking, wealth-seeking, and corrigibility.
papers.limitation:
Requires a dataset of positive and negative examples for each concept.
Steering vectors are linear, which may not capture nonlinear concepts.
Could be misused for jailbreaks or generating inappropriate content.
future_direction: Extending DISCO to other model architectures (e.g., encoder-decoder, multimodal).
Exploring nonlinear steering vectors.
Applying DISCO to more complex behaviors and real-world applications.
papers.abstract: A variety of recent methods guide large language model outputs via the inference-time addition of steering vectors to residual-stream or attention-head representations. In contrast, we propose to inject steering vectors directly into the query and value representation spaces within attention heads. We provide evidence that a greater portion of these spaces exhibit high linear discriminability of concepts --a key property motivating the use of steering vectors-- than attention head outputs. We analytically characterize the effect of our method, which we term DISentangled COmmunication (DISCO) Steering, on attention head outputs. Our analysis reveals that DISCO disentangles a strong but underutilized baseline, steering attention inputs, which implicitly modifies queries and values in a rigid manner. In contrast, DISCO's direct modulation of these components enables more granular control. We find that DISCO achieves superior performance over a number of steering vector baselines across multiple datasets on LLaMA 3.1 8B and Gemma 2 9B, with steering efficacy scoring up to 19.1% higher than the runner-up. Our results support the conclusion that the query and value spaces are powerful building blocks for steering vector methods.

papers.title: Enhancing Automated Interpretability with Output-Centric Feature Descriptions
papers.research_question: How can we generate faithful feature descriptions for LLMs by considering both the inputs that activate a feature and its causal effect on model outputs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes efficient, output-centric methods (VocabProj and TokenChange) for automatically generating feature descriptions in LLMs, and demonstrates that combining these with input-centric methods yields the most faithful descriptions across both input and output evaluations.
papers.conclusion: Output-centric methods provide efficient and effective ways to generate feature descriptions that capture causal effects, and their combination with input-centric methods yields more faithful and complete descriptions, enhancing automated interpretability pipelines.
papers.key_findings:
Output-centric feature descriptions (VocabProj, TokenChange) better capture the causal effect of a feature on model outputs than the prevalent input-centric method (MaxAct).
Combining input- and output-centric methods (ensembles) leads to the best performance on both input- and output-based evaluations of description faithfulness.
Output-centric methods are computationally efficient, requiring only a few inference passes, and can serve as a cheap alternative to MaxAct in some cases.
Output-centric descriptions can be used to find inputs that activate 'dead' features for which no activating inputs were previously identified.
Performance varies by layer and feature type, with output-based performance being lower for MLP features compared to residual stream features.
papers.abstract: Automated interpretability pipelines generate natural language descriptions for the concepts represented by features in large language models (LLMs), such as plants or the first word in a sentence. These descriptions are derived using inputs that activate the feature, which may be a dimension or a direction in the model's representation space. However, identifying activating inputs is costly, and the mechanistic role of a feature in model behavior is determined both by how inputs cause a feature to activate and by how feature activation affects outputs. Using steering evaluations, we reveal that current pipelines provide descriptions that fail to capture the causal effect of the feature on outputs. To fix this, we propose efficient, output-centric methods for automatically generating feature descriptions. These methods use the tokens weighted higher after feature stimulation or the highest weight tokens after applying the vocabulary "unembedding" head directly to the feature. Our output-centric descriptions better capture the causal effect of a feature on model outputs than input-centric descriptions, but combining the two leads to the best performance on both input and output evaluations. Lastly, we show that output-centric descriptions can be used to find inputs that activate features previously thought to be "dead".

papers.title: Improving Instruction-Following in Language Models through Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Can we efficiently extract vector representations that encode and control specific instruction-following behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can enhance instruction-following in language models by computing vectors from activations and applying them to guide generation, even without explicit instructions.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering offers a practical and scalable approach for fine-grained control in language generation.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors improve instruction adherence when no instructions are provided in the input.
Steering reinforces instruction adherence even when instructions are explicitly present.
Multiple constraints can be steered simultaneously, such as format and length.
Steering vectors computed on instruction-tuned models can transfer to improve base models.
papers.limitation:
Steering can sometimes compromise response quality, leading to nonsensical tokens or repetition.
For instructions like 'End Checker', steering vectors may fail to capture specific required sentences.
